n: Paul begins a new section (chapters 9–11) about Israel’s place in God’s plan. He solemnly affirms, with the Holy Ghost as witness to his conscience, that he speaks the truth.

f.w: I say the truth in Christ, I lie not

n: His heart carries deep, unceasing grief — because most of his fellow Jews had not accepted Jesus as the Messiah.
He could almost wish himself cut off from Christ if it would save his own people. Like Moses, Paul loved Israel enough to offer himself for them.

f.g: Greek anathema — devoted to destruction, cut off.

f.w: I could wish that myself were accursed

n: Paul lists Israel’s great privileges: adoption as God’s children, the glory of his presence, the covenants, the law, temple worship, and the promises.

f.g: The visible presence of God among Israel (the Shekinah).

n: Theirs are the patriarchs, and from them, by human descent, came the Christ — who is over all, God blessed forever.

f.g: The patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

f.w: of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came

n: This doesn’t mean God’s word has failed. Not everyone descended from Israel truly belongs to Israel. Covenant identity is about faithfulness, not just ancestry.

f.w: they are not all Israel, which are of Israel

n: Not all of Abraham’s descendants are his true children. God said the covenant line would come through Isaac — not through Ishmael.

f.w: In Isaac shall thy seed be called

n: It isn’t physical descent that makes someone God’s child; the children of the promise are counted as true descendants.
The promise was: “At this time next year I will return, and Sarah will have a son.” Isaac’s birth came by God’s word, not human ability.
Another example: Rebekah conceived twins by our father Isaac.
Before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, God made his choice — so his purpose of election would stand on his calling, not on their works.

f.g: God’s choosing — here, for a role or birthright in his covenant plan.

n: Rebekah was told, “The elder shall serve the younger.” Esau’s descendants (Edom) would serve Jacob’s (Israel).

f.w: The elder shall serve the younger

n: Paul quotes Malachi: “Jacob I loved, Esau I hated.” In Hebrew idiom, “hate” can mean “love less” or “not choose.” Malachi speaks of the nations of Israel and Edom.

f.w: Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated

n: Is God unjust, then? Certainly not!
God told Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.” Mercy is God’s free gift, never something we can demand.

f.w: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy

n: So it doesn’t ultimately depend on human desire or effort but on God, who shows mercy. Our choices matter, but salvation itself is God’s gift.

f.g: One who strives, as a runner in a race.

n: Scripture says God raised Pharaoh up to show His power and spread His name throughout the earth. Even opposition served God’s purposes.

f.w: Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up

n: So God shows mercy to whom he chooses and hardens whom he chooses. The Joseph Smith Translation of Exodus says Pharaoh hardened his own heart, preserving human agency.
An objection: then why does God still blame anyone? Who can resist his will?
Paul responds: Who are you, a human being, to talk back to God? Should a clay pot ask its maker, “Why did you make me like this?”

f.w: Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it

n: Doesn’t the potter have the right to make from one lump of clay one vessel for special use and another for ordinary use?

f.w: Hath not the potter power over the clay

n: What if God, wanting to show his judgment and power, patiently bore with “vessels of wrath” ready for destruction? His long patience leaves room to repent.
And he did it to make known his glorious riches to the “vessels of mercy” he prepared for glory.
That means us — called not only from among the Jews but also from the Gentiles.

f.w: not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles

n: As God said through Hosea: I will call those who were not my people, “my people,” and her who was not loved, “beloved.”

f.w: I will call them my people, which were not my people

n: In the very place they were told, “You are not my people,” they will be called children of the living God.

f.w: the children of the living God

n: Isaiah cried out about Israel: even if they are as numerous as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will be saved.
The Lord will carry out his word on the earth fully and swiftly.

f.w: a short work will the Lord make upon the earth

n: As Isaiah said, if the Lord of hosts hadn’t left us some descendants, we would have been wiped out like Sodom and Gomorrah.

f.g: Hebrew for “hosts” or “armies” — the Lord of heaven’s armies.

f.w: Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed

n: What’s the conclusion? Gentiles who weren’t pursuing righteousness have obtained it — the righteousness that comes by faith.

f.w: the righteousness which is of faith

n: But Israel, pursuing a law that promised righteousness, didn’t reach it.
Why? Because they pursued it through works of the law instead of faith. They stumbled over the “stumbling stone” — Christ.

As Isaiah wrote, God laid in Zion a stone that makes people stumble, a rock that offends — but whoever trusts in him will never be put to shame. Jacob in the Book of Mormon also foresaw Israel stumbling over this stone.

f.w: Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence

f.g: Will not be disappointed or put to shame.
